Every home has a small museum of unresolved possibilities.

Usually it is a drawer.

Inside: a key without a lock, a cable for a vanished device, three foreign coins, a pencil too short to hold comfortably but too long to throw away. A screw that looks important. Instructions for something that broke during a previous decade.

These objects have escaped the ordinary laws of usefulness. They survive on appeal.

*You might need me.*

And because the claim is technically impossible to disprove, they stay.

There is something tender about this. A person who would never describe themselves as an optimist will preserve a tiny metal bracket for seventeen years on the chance that one day the world will explain it.

Occasionally, the world does.

A cupboard handle comes loose. Someone searches the drawer. Beneath the dead batteries and a birthday candle shaped like a seven, the exact right screw appears.

For one glorious minute, the entire institution is vindicated.

“This,” says the keeper of the drawer, holding it up.

No further argument is necessary. The unidentified washers receive another decade of funding. The mysterious cable is granted protected status. A plastic cap, origin unknown, settles deeper into its corner.

But most objects will never have their moment. The key will remain unclaimed. The instructions will fade along their folds. Eventually someone will empty the drawer onto a table and begin making decisions.

Even then, there will probably be hesitation.

“What do you think this goes to?”

Someone will turn the little bracket over, examining its two holes and its peculiar bend. It is well made. Surely it was made for something.

“Better keep it.”

And back it goes.
